title: Office chair: get the gas spring, casters and steel out
summary: An office chair gives you a gas spring, five caster wheels, a heavy tilt spring, thick foam and a lot of steel tube and plate. Allow about 20 minutes. Two parts store energy, so slacken the tension knob first and never cut, drill or heat the gas spring.

steps.text: Turn the chair upside down on a blanket or clear floor, seat down, with room to swing a hammer. Put on safety glasses and gloves. Work where parts can't roll away.

Find the tilt-tension knob under the front of the seat (a big plastic knob or a lever) and wind it right off, usually anticlockwise, until it turns freely and the tension is gone. Set any tilt lock to free.
steps.warn: The tilt spring can hold a lot of force. If the knob is missing, seized or never goes slack, don't take the tilt mechanism apart: leave it whole and bolted.

steps.text: Pull the casters. Grip each wheel and pull it straight out of its socket in the base leg. If one is stuck, rock it side to side with a pair of pliers on the stem or lever it up with a flat screwdriver. Most stems are about 10-11 mm across, so check before you reuse them.
Remove the plastic column cover. It is a two-part telescoping sleeve around the gas spring: slide the lower part down off the cylinder, and lift or unclip the upper part.

Free the base from the gas spring. Hold the base by one leg and strike the thick hub at the centre with a hammer, glancing blows from different sides, until the base drops off the column. The column is held in a tight friction cone, not a screw. If it won't move, spray penetrating oil round the hub and wait, then try again.
steps.warn: Never cut, drill, heat or burn the gas spring, and never hit the cylinder or the polished rod: a dented tube can rupture. Wear eye protection and keep your face to one side.

steps.text: Free the top of the gas spring from the seat mechanism. Its top end is a small cone pressed into a socket in the tilt plate. Hold the cylinder with a large wrench or pipe grips (don't squeeze hard) and tap the metal plate round the socket sharply with a hammer from several sides until the cone lets go. If it won't come, leave it in the mechanism: a gas spring with a steel plate on top is still a gas spring.

Separate the seat, back and arms from the mechanism. Undo the four bolts under the seat (hex key or socket, usually 5/16 in or M8), then the bolts that hold the arms and the back uprights. Keep all bolts, washers and nuts sorted by size in a jar or tin.

Strip the foam and fabric. The foam is stapled or glued to a plastic or plywood pan: lever the staples out with pliers and peel the foam away. Cut the fabric into large pieces along the seams. Keep the foam and fabric dry.

Check the gas spring. Stand it upright on the floor with the polished rod up and lean your weight on the rod: a good one holds you at full height and doesn't sink. Look for oil on the rod or a tube that is dented or deeply rusted. Handle the polished rod carefully: scratches ruin the seal.

Sort and store: keep the gas spring upright out of sun and heat, the casters in a bag, the tilt mechanism whole with its spring, and the steel in one pile. Check the pile for sharp edges and wear gloves.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Gas spring.** A sealed, pressurised cylinder with a stroke of 10-15 cm that carries a person's weight. Use it to hold up a lid or hatch, to lift a heavy trapdoor or shutter, or to give a stool or workbench adjustable height. Mount it with pipe clamps or in a matching tapered socket. Keep it away from heat and never weld near it.
- **Casters.** Five wheels with stems. Use them on a hand cart, a dolly or a platform for a heavy tank or tool chest (see build_hand_cart). Each carries only a modest load, so spread the weight over all five and keep the load low.
- **Tilt spring.** A heavy coil, useful as a return spring for a lever or a latch. Only remove it from its mechanism once it is fully slack.
- **Foam.** Seat cushions, knee pads, bedding pads and insulation under a roof or a floor. Polyurethane foam burns fast with a poisonous smoke: keep it away from flames and stoves.
- **Steel.** The column, tilt plate and arms make brackets, handles and frames. The five-star base is strong and spins: use it as a base for a stool, a rotating stand or a small table.
- **Fabric.** Mesh and upholstery cloth make a sieve, a screen or a patch.
- **Bolts.** M8 and 5/16 in bolts and screws: sort them and keep them.

## Variations

- Cheap chairs have no tension knob and a simple plate with a smaller spring. They are quicker to take apart.
- Gaming and executive chairs have heavier steel frames and stronger gas springs. The big seat pan may be plywood.
- Heavy-duty chairs use a bigger cylinder; read any label on it before you handle it.
- Mesh chairs have a plastic frame and no foam.
- Nylon bases are strong glass-filled plastic; aluminium bases are lighter and stiffer.

## What to leave

- A seized tilt mechanism with the spring still under tension.
- A damaged or leaking gas spring.
